Recent findings suggest that but, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.

The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.

He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.

Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.

The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.

Sources indicate that it hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.

But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal's key players.

People don't know full story behind England exile - White.

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages.

"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never noted anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.

The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.

After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.

His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.

That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.

Industry observers note that white, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.

"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White said of his return to England.

He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.

This upcoming era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.

And with three of his Arsenal team-mates on the pitch as England won the game, and Bukayo Saka to return, White brings the positives of the cohesion of a club side to Tuchel's team.

Arsenal supporters will not be surprised by White's excellent performances for England.

Such is the importance of White, the Gunners attack does not flow as freely when he is not in the side to link up with Martin Odegaard and Saka as he relentlessly produces overlapping runs - a trait he showed when he scored England's third in Madrid.

White is a unique character within football, and has even remarked he doesn't watch the game away from the training ground, but his passion for his profession cannot be doubted.

Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.
  • Industry observers note that the annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

Industry observers note that the annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Industry observers note that leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

Recent findings suggest that but back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows.".

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this. -- November 18, 2026 York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3November 18, 2026.

This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively rapidly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, Newly introduced Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

"But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog.".

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

According to recent reports, "One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

さきほど、しし座流星群の大火球が流れました。2026年11月19日4時35分2秒に、平塚から北の低い空に向けたカメラでとらえた様子です。緑色のアフターグローからオレンジ色の永続痕まで、美しく色を変化させました。 https://t.co/Q5ihqCPtX2November 18, 2026.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

昨夜から今朝にかけて捉えた流星は正味92個でした。 11/18 22:17 〜 11/19 05:40 埼玉県中央から #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 https://t.co/jRzsHdQ7MVNovember 19, 2026.

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

昨夜の流星とスプライト、初めて同じタイミングで撮れた。 11/19 02:19:36 埼玉県中央から北西の空 #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 #スプライト https://t.co/LBipTuoM0LNovember 19, 2026.

The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky.

It has been revealed that meteors from last night/this morning. Cropped to show detail. A lot of possible Leonids. The Leonid meteor shower is active and peaks the night of 11/17-11/18. https://t.co/s7YsvKdvECNovember 15, 2026.

In a recent development, A likely Leonid meteor from yesterday morning. The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Good luck if you go out to watch. https://t.co/xxbEV32NQlNovember 17, 2026.

According to recent reports, if the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

Editor's Note: If you snap an impressive night sky photo and would like to share it with Space.com's readers, send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

In a recent development, daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#24812. Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca

Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • In a recent development, although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • In a recent development, polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

In a recent development, although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

In a recent development, polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how notable the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

It has been revealed that the discovery shows that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

Industry observers note that dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

Recent findings suggest that for roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

However, the most crucial finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

Recent findings suggest that this suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

Polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

One example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

The problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, fresh ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

In a recent development, prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

Sources indicate that the discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An vital question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

Researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is right now participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

Recent findings suggest that the findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

It has been revealed that materials provided by MARUM - Center for Marine Environmental Sciences, University of Bremen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Sources indicate that ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

It has been revealed that “Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he stated, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”.

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

It has been revealed that the Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice.

Recent findings suggest that ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Sources indicate that strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he stated on Facebook.

Industry observers note that the state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha remarked that Alshebl’s victory highlighted that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Industry observers note that not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and mentioned he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last.

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”.

Industry observers note that for the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

If the surgeon could prescribe one piece of advice, it would be to place that bond above all else. "The bottom line is this: I would do anything for her. Climb any mountain, take any bullet—in the chest, too, by the way. I might do things that justifiably make her really angry at me, but I would never let anything block me from delivering my love to her," he swore. If you appreciate how valuable marriage is to your long-term happiness, he continued, "You will never let anyone touch it.".

ABC News reporter Roberts isn't always one for chit-chat. "I don't like the check-in," she explaind. "If you're calling just to say, 'So, what's up?' no, I do not like that." Everyone's favorite TV weatherman, however, is a phone guy. And after years of chafing against his frequent calls, a pal proposed something that changed her stance. "One friend noted to me, 'Did you ever think that maybe he just feels comfortable when he hears your voice, because that tells him that all is right in the world?'" she recounted. "And I thought, 'That's very sweet. I'd never thought about it in that way. And if it means something to him, then it should mean something to me.'"Now, she said, "I have learned to take a breath and say, 'Sweetie, I've got some stuff going on, but what's going on with you? Great. I'm glad to hear from you. Got to go. Talk to you later. Love you.' That makes all the difference in the world to him, and it doesn't kill me for two minutes to be nice and sweet." They celebrated their 29th anniversary in September 2024.

It has been revealed that the building blocks for their nearly 30-year union began back in their newlywed days, when any fight—one involved the Riverdale actor throwing the talk show host's ring out the window—felt like it could be it. "Early in a marriage, it's easy to let little things become substantial things—whether it's financial strain or career strain or you have kids and you're sleep-deprived," espoused the LIVE With Kelly and Ryan star. "But Mark taught me to walk away and take a breath. That's when you figure out that it's not a marriage-defining moment."Some hard-earned wisdom, to be sure, but now the parents of three are reaping the benefits. "Anytime you see a couple who seems truly happy, you can bet they've gone through some crazy, crazy stuff together and they've survived," he stated. "That's something to be proud of.".

She's an introvert, she remarked, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts.".

According to recent reports, you don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having mentioned hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship.".

Judges Judy Sheindlin & Jerry Sheindlin.

Few things are more on brand than former Fresh York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and quickly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday plans. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are.".

According to recent reports, the Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic.".

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor noted his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening.".

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Empire State Building glowed in glittering gold last night (Nov. 17) to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hitting one light-day from Earth. And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display.

In a recent development, today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space.

To celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in Latest York City lit up in gold. This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

And the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. The Space Needle in Seattle, Washington, and both the Willis Tower and the Skydeck Chicago in Chicago, Illinois have all been illuminated gold to mark the milestone.

Sources indicate that the Golden Record that these gold glowing buildings are referencing serves as an inanimate ambassador for Earth, carrying information about humanity, our planet, the other species who live here, the languages we speak, the music we listen to and so much more. It even includes instructions for building a record player to play the record.

The Voyager mission has, and continues to, make incredible scientific discoveries and observations throughout our solar system and now in interstellar space. But this Golden Record provides an additional aspect to the mission that connects us here on Earth to whatever unknown life may exist out there.

If some sort of life forms out in the cosmos were to ever come across Voyager and its Golden Record at any point in the distant future, they might learn a little bit about our small blue dot.

When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. Tech Report: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.
  • The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.
  • The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

Sources indicate that in the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a tech giant with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued.".

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money.".

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction.".

Recent findings suggest that "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie.".

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers strategy to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

Sources indicate that with many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI prepares, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

Recent findings suggest that there are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs.".

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to glitch newly introduced AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have unveiled deals worth $67 billion.

Rees mentioned another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer upcoming clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

Industry observers note that the newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

According to recent reports, the latest discovery provides an important breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," remarked lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

Sources indicate that A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," stated Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

After the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Sources indicate that both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

Dr. McSweeney remarked, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

  • Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Substantial Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Substantial Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

It has been revealed that however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Massive 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green indicates that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on concerns impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he notes.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, claims Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “Latest Major 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, indicates Green.

According to recent reports, as well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “Newly introduced Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

Industry observers note that “I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The Upcoming Massive 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of concerns covered by the book.

#24797. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1704 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings raise notable questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But latest research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

Recent findings suggest that the findings raise notable questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

According to recent reports, the study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

It has been revealed that deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

According to recent reports, in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an important role in carrying away waste products.

Sources indicate that that earlier discovery led to a newly introduced question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

In a recent development, previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially vital.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

The researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

Sources indicate that the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings revealed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

Sources indicate that the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

Recent findings suggest that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

Recent findings suggest that to measure this response, the researchers demonstrated volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

Sources indicate that in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

It has been revealed that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group revealed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

It has been revealed that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

It has been revealed that "Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes indicates. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have important implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

It has been revealed that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants revealed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

It has been revealed that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

According to recent reports, while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

"It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

‘Incredibly frustrating’: prestigious fellowship applications close in just 21 hours

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.
  • It has been revealed that swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship.
  • After sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.

It has been revealed that swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship. On 14 November, he stayed up through the night completing the form and coordinating with referees across different time zones.

After sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking. When he returned to submit it at around 8.50 p.m., applications had closed. The fellowship had reached its limit of 800 applications within 21 hours of opening.

In a recent development, chowbey is not alone. Many researchers around the world found themselves unable to submit applications last Sunday and took to social media to vent their annoyance.

“It is incredibly frustrating to invest so much time and effort into developing a strong scientific project, only to discover that the timing of the application process may put some researchers at a disadvantage — especially when you open the system on Sunday and close it the same day,” wrote Ida Skubis, an AI researcher at Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland, on the social-media platform LinkedIn.

In a recent development, the Humboldt Research Fellowships support researchers from abroad to conduct research in Germany, providing €3,000 (US$3,300) a month for postdoctoral researchers and €3,600 a month for experienced researchers. Fellowships can last for 6–24 months for postdocs and 6–18 months for experienced researchers.

It has been revealed that the fellowships and awards are recognized internationally, which is why they are so competitive, notes Marcela Hernández, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a former fellow. “Being a Humboldtian is a mark of academic distinction. It has an exceptional international network.”.

Industry observers note that A spokesperson for the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in Bonn, Germany, stated in a statement to Nature that it had not anticipated that the application cap would be reached within 24 hours of opening. The foundation introduced the cap this year because it has seen a large increase in applications since 2024. It holds application rounds in March, July and November.

In a recent development, the spokesperson stated that as more researchers have used AI to help prepare their applications more quickly, the volume of applications has increased. Humboldt does not prohibit the use of generative AI in applications, nor are applicants required to declare AI use.

In a recent development, simon Hammann, a chemist at the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart, Germany, supported a research proposal as a prospectiveacademic host for someone who was able to submit their application successfully. He claims that opening the call on a Sunday disadvantaged researchers with family and caring responsibilities. “That should definitely be changed.”.

The Humboldt spokesperson said that the foundation advertises the date when applications will open, but that unfortunately the date fell on a Sunday this time.

“We recognize the impact this had on those who were unable to apply, particularly given the challenges of coordinating availability over a weekend. We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” the spokesperson remarked.

They added: “We will take this as an opportunity to continue reflecting on and improving our processes” to “find a transparent and fair solution”.

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • Industry observers note that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

Industry observers note that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A new study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

Planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

On Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

Earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

According to recent reports, uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

Sources indicate that "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," remarked Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

Ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

Their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

According to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

Sources indicate that "Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," remarked Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

Industry observers note that these dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

Recent findings suggest that researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

Recent findings suggest that auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an notable stepping stone," stated Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

It has been revealed that the research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the fresh dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

Even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require newly introduced spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the moon shines close to the ringed giant Saturn after sunset tonight (Nov. 20), presenting a spectacular naked-eye display as the stars of the Great Square of Pegasus twinkle nearby.

It has been revealed that saturn's steady light will appear a little over 5 degrees from the 82%-lit moon in the southeastern sky after the sun dips below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length.

Moonlight will hide fainter stars from view, though you should be able to spot Algenib, Markab, Alpheratz and Scheat arrayed in a diamond formation above the lunar disk, marking out the asterism of the Great Square of Pegasus in the November sky.

The moon will present a spectacular target through the eyepiece of a 6-inch telescope, as the terminator line separating night from day creeps ever closer to its western edge. It's a great time to explore the 110 km-wide Gassendi Crater on the edge of Mare Humorum as its eastern rim and central peaks throw intense shadows across its interior.

Slewing your telescope over to Saturn will reveal details and subtle variations in the cloud surface of the gas giant, along with its iconic ring system, which is gradually becoming more visible following its ring plane crossing in March 2025.

Depending on viewing conditions, you may also notice a shoal of bright, star-like points of light surrounding Saturn's disk, which represent the large moons Titan, Dione, Tethys, Rhea and Iapetus.

It has been revealed that interested in seeing the planets of the solar system up close for yourself? Then be sure to check out our picks of the best telescopes available in 2026, including the Celestron NexStar 8SE, which we rate as the best motorized scope out there.
